summary: Proposes a standard syntax for Network Standard Data Pathnames: a uniform way to say where a collection of bits lives on the network. It was replaced by RFC 645.

eli5.summary: Every computer named its files differently. This proposes one way to write a file's full address so anyone can find it. A later paper replaced it.

subtitle: Proposed standard syntax for specifying file locations across the network.

tldr.problem: Each computer system on ARPANET used its own syntax to specify file paths, making it difficult for users and programs to access files on remote systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 615 proposes a unified syntax using field keys (NETWORK, HOST, PERIPHERAL, DIRECTORY, FILE, TYPE, SITEPARM) separated by delimiters, allowing users to specify a complete path that any host could parse.
tldr.outcome: The proposal aimed to let users refer to files across the network with a single standard syntax, though it was later replaced by RFC 645.

facts.label: Field types
facts.value: 7 (network, host, peripheral, directory, file, type, siteparm)

today: RFC 615 proposed a standard that was later superseded by RFC 645.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 615 proposes a standard syntax for Network Standard Data Pathnames (NSDP): a uniform way to specify where a collection of bits lives on the ARPA Network. The motivation is that users who work across multiple computers, and programs that access data at different sites, need a single syntax they can use everywhere.
sections.eli5: When you use many computers, you have to learn each one's weird way of naming files. This proposes one way that would work everywhere.

sections.title: The NSDP Format
sections.content: The syntax uses field keys and delimiters. A message starts with a percent sign (%) and contains a series of fields such as NETWORK (or N), HOST (H), PERIPHERAL (P), DIRECTORY (D), FILE (F), TYPE (T), and SITEPARM (S). Each field has a key, a left delimiter, the actual name, and a right delimiter. Matching bracket pairs like < > or [ ] can serve as delimiters. For example, %H[ISI]D<DCROCKER>F(MESSAGE) refers to a file MESSAGE owned by DCROCKER at ISI.
sections.eli5: The format is like a postal address: first the network, then the computer, then the storage device, then folders, then the filename, separated by special characters.

sections.title: Field Definitions
sections.content: Network names the network (currently only ARPA is defined). Host specifies a machine by name, nickname or number. Peripheral names the storage device (disk, tape, printer). Directory is a folder. File is the base filename. Type is an optional file extension. Siteparm allows site-specific attributes like access protection or version numbers. Fields are order-dependent, and many may be omitted in favor of defaults (ARPA for network, the local host for host, ONLINE disk for peripheral).
sections.eli5: Each field means one part of the path. Some are required, some can be left out and the computer will guess.
